title: AI cuts build time but that doesn't mean the game is ready to ship
author: Sloptrawler
selftext:
Follow-up to my last post about Steam getting 86–200 new games a day \[[link](https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/comments/1y2xvq2/steam_is_getting_86200_new_games_a_day_the_number/)\]. A lot of the comments landed on “marketing matters more now,” so I charted what the pipeline actually looks like with and without AI. This is not a doomer post.

The short version: AI speeds up prototyping and some of the build, but it didn’t add any new players. Steam has roughly the same audience it had before, and reaching them takes the same time and effort it always did: devlogs, a demo, Next Fest, creators, getting wishlists to pile up. AI just put a lot more games between you and those players (Next Fest went from 887 games in June 2023 to 7,240 in October 2026). So if you launch as soon as the build is done, you’ve cut the slow part short, not the build. The time you saved building is better spent on that slow part.

The mistake I keep seeing: finish the build, put up a Steam page a few weeks out, launch with a few hundred wishlists. The usual advice is a page up 6–12 months before launch and \~7k wishlists, so marketing has to start while you’re still building.

Also worth knowing: if AI art, audio or text ships in your game, you have to disclose it on your store page. AI coding tools don’t need to be disclosed (Valve changed this in January 2026).

**Before anyone says it:**

“The bar widths are made up.” They’re my estimate, not measured data, and the chart says so. The ratio is the point. If your split looks different, tell me what it is.

“Slotbound did fine.” It did, and it deserves the credit. But the teaser went viral over the summer, the demo was up by July, and it had months of wishlists and buzz before launching in November. That’s the marketing track on this chart, not a way around it. Breakouts like that are worth studying but really hard to copy.

“A good game will find its audience.” Probably, but it has to get seen first. More games means more noise between your game and the people who’d love it. The cream still floats to the top but since the sea is deeper it takes a lot longer to do it.

“I don’t have a marketing budget.” Most of what’s on the chart costs time, not money: devlogs, a demo, Next Fest, posting here, reaching out to creators. Translation counts too. AI is good at it now, and more languages put you in front of more players.

“AI will keep getting better, so the build box will shrink to nothing.” Maybe, but the marketing box won’t. Building gets cheaper for everyone, the number of players stays about the same, and reaching them still takes months.

“7k is outdated.” It’s historic best practice, not a guarantee. Chris Zukowski’s 2026 benchmarks put a solid launch around 8k, and plenty of games launch below that.

Sources in the first comment.

(Had Claude help clean up the writing. Same as last time, just showing what the data says.)

How far out did you put your Steam page up, and would you do it differently?

P.S. I do have skin in the game. My own project is a Shandalar/MTG-inspired roguelite built around cards I’ve been noodling on for years: [Goo World: Primordial Sea](https://sloptrawler.itch.io/goo-world-primordial-sea). Right now it’s a free alpha card game on itch, built with Claude writing all the code, Godot engine with Lua scripted cards and Nano Banana placeholder art. No Steam page yet. That’s next, and I’m following this exact timeline myself, so the page goes up well before launch. I’ll let you know how it goes =)

comments.author: Sloptrawler
comments.body:
Sources for the chart:

\- Wishlist benchmarks and Steam page timing (Chris Zukowski): [https://howtomarketagame.com/2022/09/25/archive-how-many-wishlists-should-i-have-when-i-launch-my-game/](https://howtomarketagame.com/2022/09/25/archive-how-many-wishlists-should-i-have-when-i-launch-my-game/)

\- 2026 wishlist tiers (5k / 8k / 50k / 90k): [https://www.steampageanalyzer.com/blog/how-many-wishlists-before-launch](https://www.steampageanalyzer.com/blog/how-many-wishlists-before-launch)

\- Next Fest growth, 887 to 7,240 games: [https://howtomarketagame.com/?p=7168](https://howtomarketagame.com/?p=7168)

\- Valve's January 2026 AI disclosure update: [https://www.pcgamer.com/software/ai/steam-updates-ai-disclosure-form-to-specify-that-its-focused-on-ai-generated-content-that-is-consumed-by-players-not-efficiency-tools-used-behind-the-scenes/](https://www.pcgamer.com/software/ai/steam-updates-ai-disclosure-form-to-specify-that-its-focused-on-ai-generated-content-that-is-consumed-by-players-not-efficiency-tools-used-behind-the-scenes/)

\- Slotbound's viral teaser and launch: [https://ixbt.games/en/news/2026/11/14/v-stean-vysel-pravilnyi-neiroslop-azartnyi-rogalik-slotbound-privlek-tysiaci-igrokov-i-polucil-ocen-polozitelnye-otzyvy.html](https://ixbt.games/en/news/2026/11/14/v-stean-vysel-pravilnyi-neiroslop-azartnyi-rogalik-slotbound-privlek-tysiaci-igrokov-i-polucil-ocen-polozitelnye-otzyvy.html)

comments.author: teejayaiartdirector
comments.body: Why would you ship a game?! AI made all digital content and games to have zero value! Just make games for your own enjoyment but don't expect to make any money of it! 😂

replies.author: Sloptrawler
replies.body: You can, and that’s mostly what I’m doing with mine. Free and shared with a community is a great reason to ship. “Zero value” isn’t what the numbers show though: 608 games from 2025 hit 1,000+ reviews. It’s a lot harder now, not impossible.

comments.author: Sloptrawler
comments.body:
Sorry to hear that, launch day flopping hurts, especially when you believe in the game. What you're describing is basically what I was getting at: you need a great product AND great marketing AND some luck now. I think that's true across most media right now, not just games.

If you're up for sharing, how did you market your game before launch? Your first game making five figures and this one struggling would be a really useful comparison for people here.

comments.author: mentiondesk
comments.body: Putting your Steam page up early really does give you time to build wishlists and momentum, especially with so much noise on Steam now. Tracking where your potential fans are talking can make a big difference too. I started using ParseStream to catch relevant threads in real time across different communities and it helped me join conversations while interest was still fresh.

comments.author: Sloptrawler
comments.body: Sorry man, that's brutal. A year of promotion plus a PC Gamer show versus 2 months and 150 wishlists is pretty much the whole chart in one comparison.
